title: Handling Missing Data V - MICE
abstract:
Multivariate Imputation by Chained Equations — the most accurate of the
standard imputation methods, and the one that requires understanding the
missingness mechanism to justify. This document works the seven-step algorithm
from the notes, explains why the iteration converges, shows what
multiple imputation adds over the single-imputation version scikit-learn
implements, covers the choice of estimator inside the loop, and gives the
practical guidance on cost, convergence checking and when the simpler methods are
the correct answer.

blocks.t: The Mechanism It Assumes
From the notes

items: People didn't fill age somewhere, or name

blocks.t: MICE works best for MAR and is more accurate.

The three mechanisms were introduced in Topic 23. The reason they reappear here
is that MICE is the method whose validity depends on which one you have.
Under MAR, missingness depends on columns you can observe — and MICE's whole
strategy is to condition on those observed columns. That is precisely the
situation it was designed for.

What MICE can do
Why
rows: Works, but simpler methods are unbiased too
Nothing to condition on; you only gain efficiency
The dependence is on observed columns, which is exactly what the chained regressions model
Reduces but does not remove the bias

blocks.t: The Algorithm
The steps, from the notes

items: Pick one column at a time, treat it as the target ($y$).
Use the other columns as input ($X$).
Train a model to predict the missing values.
Replace the picked column's values with the predicted ones.

Repeat steps 1–6 until the difference between the imputed and predicted
 value is near 0.

blocks.t:
Iteratively fills values using the other features, instead of simple
averages.

blocks.cap:
The chained-equations loop. Each column is imputed by a model trained
 on all the others, and the whole cycle repeats until the fills stop changing.

blocks.t: Worked, on three columns
Suppose $x_1$, $x_2$, $x_3$ each have gaps.

head: Round 0

Fill every gap with the column mean. Nothing is modelled yet;
this is only a starting point so that no cell is empty.
rows:
Set $x_1$'s originally-missing cells back to NaN. Fit
$x_1 \sim f(x_2,x_3)$ on the rows where $x_1$ is observed. Predict the missing
$x_1$ and write the predictions in.

Now do the same for $x_2$, using the updated $x_1$ and the current $x_3$.

Then $x_3$, using the updated $x_1$ and $x_2$.

Repeat. Each column is now predicted from better estimates of
the others than in cycle 1.

When the imputed values stop changing between cycles — "the
difference between imputed and predicted value is near 0".

blocks.t: Why the iteration is necessary, and why it converges

The target is a draw from the conditional distribution
$P(x_j \mid x_{-j})$ for every $j$. But $x_{-j}$ itself contains imputed values,
so the conditional you are sampling from is only as good as the current fills —
which is why one pass is not enough.

The procedure is a Gibbs-sampler-like scheme: it cycles through the conditionals
$P(x_1\mid x_{-1}), P(x_2\mid x_{-2}),\ldots$ Under regularity conditions this
converges to the joint distribution $P(x_1,\ldots,x_p)$. In practice convergence
is fast — 5 to 10 cycles is typical — because each column's model improves
monotonically as its inputs improve.

The formal justification is exact only when the conditionals are mutually
compatible (they correspond to some genuine joint distribution). With arbitrary
estimators they may not be, which is why MICE is sometimes described as
"incompatible Gibbs sampling" — it works extremely well empirically without a
complete theoretical guarantee.
Why It Beats the Alternatives

blocks.cap:
The correlation matrices. Mean imputation flattens the structure
 towards zero — exactly the attenuation derived in Topic 24. KNN partially
 recovers it. MICE reconstructs it closely, because it explicitly models each
 column as a function of the others.

blocks.t: Choosing the Estimator Inside the Loop

The "model" in step 4 is a parameter. scikit-learn defaults to
BayesianRidge, which is fast and stable, but any regressor works.

rows: Linear, regularised, fast, has a natural noise estimate. The right default
Captures non-linearity and interactions; this is roughly what the R package missForest does. Much slower
Local, non-parametric; makes MICE behave like an iterated KNN imputer
Similar to Extra Trees; robust but slow

blocks.t: Categorical columns need care

The chained-equations idea extends naturally to categorical targets — you fit a
classifier rather than a regressor for those columns. R's mice
package does this automatically. scikit-learn's IterativeImputer is
regression-only, so you must encode categoricals to integers first and round the
output, or use a library such as miceforest.
Single vs Multiple Imputation
The "M" in MICE means multiple, and sklearn's default is not

The original method runs the whole chain $m$ times with different random draws,
producing $m$ complete datasets. You then fit your model $m$ times and combine the
results using Rubin's rules:

The between-imputation term is the point: it propagates the uncertainty
about what the missing values were into your final standard errors. Single
imputation — which is what IterativeImputer does by default — pretends
the imputed values are known facts and therefore understates uncertainty, exactly
as mean imputation does.

For prediction this rarely matters: you want one number per row, and a
model's accuracy is judged on held-out data. For inference — confidence
intervals, $p$-values, effect sizes — it matters a great deal. Set
sample_posterior=True and vary the seed to approximate proper multiple
imputation.
Practical Guidance

head: Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: Most accurate of the standard methods
Convergence is not guaranteed and should be checked
The estimator is swappable, so it can capture non-linearity
Regression-only in sklearn; categoricals need work
Single imputation by default understates uncertainty

blocks.t: When not to use it

If the columns are nearly independent, there is nothing for the chained
regressions to exploit and MICE reduces to an expensive mean. If under 5% of
values are missing, the difference between methods is usually smaller than the
noise in your evaluation. Check the correlation matrix and the missing rate before
reaching for it — and always compare against median imputation by
cross-validation rather than assuming the sophisticated method wins.
Code

import numpy as np, pandas as pd, time
from sklearn.experimental import enable_iterative_imputer   # REQUIRED import
from sklearn.impute import IterativeImputer, SimpleImputer, KNNImputer
from sklearn.linear_model import BayesianRidge, LogisticRegression
from sklearn.ensemble import ExtraTreesRegressor
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsRegressor
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score, train_test_split

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 2000
x1 = rng.normal(0, 1, n)
x2 = 0.85 * x1 + rng.normal(0, .4, n)          # correlated
x3 = 0.60 * x1 - 0.50 * x2 + rng.normal(0, .4, n)
X_true = np.c_[x1, x2, x3]

M = rng.random(X_true.shape) < .22              # MCAR for the demo
X = X_true.copy(); X[M] = np.nan
print(f"missing: {M.mean():.0%} of cells, "
      f"{(M.any(axis=1)).mean():.0%} of rows affected")

# =====================================================================
# 1. THE ALGORITHM, IMPLEMENTED FROM THE NOTES' SEVEN STEPS
# =====================================================================
def mice_scratch(X, max_iter=10, tol=1e-3, verbose=True):
    X = X.copy()
    missing = np.isnan(X)

    # STEP 1: fill all NaN with the column mean
    col_mean = np.nanmean(X, axis=0)
    for j in range(X.shape[1]):
        X[missing[:, j], j] = col_mean[j]

    for it in range(max_iter):
        prev = X[missing].copy()

        # STEP 6: do this for ALL columns
        for j in range(X.shape[1]):
            if not missing[:, j].any():
                continue
            # STEP 2: treat column j as the target
            # STEP 3: the OTHER columns are the input
            others = [c for c in range(X.shape[1]) if c != j]
            obs = ~missing[:, j]

            # STEP 4: train a model on the rows where j IS observed
            model = BayesianRidge().fit(X[obs][:, others], X[obs, j])

            # STEP 5: replace the missing values with the predictions
            X[missing[:, j], j] = model.predict(X[missing[:, j]][:, others])

        # STEP 7: stop when the change is near zero
        delta = np.abs(X[missing] - prev).mean()
        if verbose:
            print(f"  iter {it+1:2d}  mean change {delta:.6f}")
        if delta < tol:
            break
    return X

print("scratch MICE:")
scratch = mice_scratch(X, max_iter=8)
print("scratch MAE:", np.abs(scratch[M] - X_true[M]).mean().round(4))

# =====================================================================
# 2. SKLEARN'S VERSION
# =====================================================================
mice = IterativeImputer(max_iter=15, random_state=0, tol=1e-3)
filled = mice.fit_transform(X)
print("sklearn MAE:", np.abs(filled[M] - X_true[M]).mean().round(4))
print("iterations actually run:", mice.n_iter_)

# =====================================================================
# 3. COMPARED WITH EVERYTHING ELSE
# =====================================================================
methods = {
    "mean":         SimpleImputer(strategy="mean"),
    "median":       SimpleImputer(strategy="median"),
    "KNN (k=5)":    KNNImputer(n_neighbors=5),
    "MICE":         IterativeImputer(max_iter=15, random_state=0),
    "MICE + trees": IterativeImputer(
                        estimator=ExtraTreesRegressor(n_estimators=25,
                                                      random_state=0),
                        max_iter=8, random_state=0),
}
print(f"\n{'method':14s} {'MAE':>8s} {'time':>9s}")
for name, m in methods.items():
    t = time.perf_counter(); v = m.fit_transform(X); el = time.perf_counter() - t
    print(f"{name:14s} {np.abs(v[M]-X_true[M]).mean():8.4f} {el:8.3f}s")

# =====================================================================
# 4. CORRELATION STRUCTURE -- what MICE actually buys you
# =====================================================================
def corr_error(v):
    return np.abs(np.corrcoef(v, rowvar=False)
                  - np.corrcoef(X_true, rowvar=False)).sum()
print(f"\ncorrelation-matrix error:")
for name, m in methods.items():
    print(f"  {name:14s} {corr_error(m.fit_transform(X)):.4f}")
# mean imputation is far and away the worst -- it flattens everything.

# =====================================================================
# 5. CHECKING CONVERGENCE -- do NOT assume it happened
# =====================================================================
traces = []
for it in range(1, 16):
    v = IterativeImputer(max_iter=it, random_state=0, tol=1e-12).fit_transform(X)
    traces.append(v[M].mean())
print("\nmean of imputed values by iteration:",
      np.round(traces, 4)[:8], "...")
deltas = np.abs(np.diff(traces))
print("converged at iteration:", int(np.argmax(deltas < 1e-4)) + 2
      if (deltas < 1e-4).any() else "NOT CONVERGED -- raise max_iter")

# =====================================================================
# 6. MULTIPLE imputation -- the "M" that sklearn's default drops
# =====================================================================
m_datasets = []
for seed in range(5):
    imp = IterativeImputer(max_iter=10, random_state=seed,
                           sample_posterior=True)    # draw, do not just predict
    m_datasets.append(imp.fit_transform(X))

y = (0.8*x1 + 0.5*x2 - 0.3*x3 + rng.normal(0, .5, n) > 0).astype(int)
coefs = np.array([LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000).fit(d, y).coef_[0]
                  for d in m_datasets])

theta_bar = coefs.mean(axis=0)                       # Rubin's pooled estimate
between  = coefs.var(axis=0, ddof=1)                 # BETWEEN-imputation variance
print("\npooled coefficients :", theta_bar.round(3))
print("between-imputation SD:", np.sqrt(between).round(4))
# Single imputation reports zero for that second line -- it pretends the
# imputed values were known. For INFERENCE that is a real understatement.

# =====================================================================
# 7. WHEN MICE IS NOT WORTH IT -- independent columns
# =====================================================================
Z_true = rng.normal(0, 1, (1500, 6))                 # no correlation at all
Mz = rng.random(Z_true.shape) < .22
Z = Z_true.copy(); Z[Mz] = np.nan
print(f"\nindependent columns:")
print("  median MAE:", np.abs(SimpleImputer(strategy='median')
        .fit_transform(Z)[Mz] - Z_true[Mz]).mean().round(4))
print("  MICE   MAE:", np.abs(IterativeImputer(max_iter=10, random_state=0)
        .fit_transform(Z)[Mz] - Z_true[Mz]).mean().round(4))
# Essentially identical. Check the correlation matrix BEFORE reaching for MICE.

# =====================================================================
# 8. IN A PIPELINE, AND FITTED ON TRAIN ONLY
# =====================================================================
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=.25, random_state=0)

for name, imp in [("median", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),
                  ("KNN",    KNNImputer(n_neighbors=5)),
                  ("MICE",   IterativeImputer(max_iter=10, random_state=0))]:
    pipe = Pipeline([("imp", imp), ("sc", StandardScaler()),
                     ("clf", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))])
    cv = cross_val_score(pipe, X_tr, y_tr, cv=5, scoring="roc_auc").mean()
    te = pipe.fit(X_tr, y_tr).score(X_te, y_te)
    print(f"{name:8s} cv auc {cv:.4f}   test acc {te:.4f}")
# The imputer is FITTED on the training folds only. Its internal regressions
# are learned parameters exactly like a mean, and must not see test data.
Summary
Everything on one page

items:
MICE = Multivariate Imputation by Chained Equations. It
 works best for MAR and is more accurate.

The steps: (1) fill all NaN with mean/median; (2) pick one
 column at a time and treat it as the target $y$; (3) use the other
 columns as input $X$; (4) train a model to predict the missing values;
 (5) replace the picked column's values with the predicted ones; (6) do
 this for all columns; (7) repeat until the difference between imputed and
 predicted is near 0.

It iteratively fills values using the other features, instead of
 simple averages — which is why it reconstructs the correlation
 structure that mean imputation flattens.

The iteration is a Gibbs-sampler-like cycle through the conditionals
 $P(x_j \mid x_{-j})$; 5–10 cycles is typically enough.

The estimator inside the loop is swappable: BayesianRidge by
 default, tree estimators for non-linearity.

sklearn's IterativeImputer does single imputation by
 default. True multiple imputation runs the chain $m$ times and pools with
 Rubin's rules, which is what propagates uncertainty — essential for
 inference, rarely necessary for prediction.

Not worth it when columns are independent or very little is missing.
 Compare against the median by cross-validation.

blocks.t: Questions you will actually be asked
Q. Explain MICE in one paragraph.

Fill every gap with the column mean as a starting point. Then take one column at
a time, blank out its originally-missing cells, fit a model predicting that
column from all the others on the rows where it is observed, and write the
predictions back. Do this for every column, then repeat the whole cycle until the
imputed values stop changing. It replaces a single unconditional average with a
set of conditional models that inform each other.
Q. Why does it need to iterate?

Because when you impute column 1 you use columns 2 and 3, which are themselves
still filled with crude means. Once columns 2 and 3 improve, column 1's model has
better inputs and can be improved in turn. The cycle propagates information until
it stabilises.
Q. Which missingness mechanism does MICE assume?

MAR — missingness depends on the observed data. That is exactly what
conditioning on the other columns can capture. It is unbiased under MCAR too
(and merely more efficient), and it reduces but does not eliminate bias under
MNAR.

Q. What is the difference between IterativeImputer and true
MICE?

IterativeImputer produces one completed dataset — single imputation.
True MICE produces $m$ datasets from $m$ runs with different random draws, fits
the model $m$ times, and pools the results with Rubin's rules so that the
uncertainty about the missing values propagates into the standard errors.
Q. When would you use median imputation instead?

When under about 5% is missing, when the columns are nearly independent, when
the dataset is large enough that the extra fits are prohibitive, or when the
model is a gradient-boosted tree that handles missingness natively. Always verify
the choice by cross-validation rather than assuming the sophisticated method
wins.
Q. How do you know MICE has converged?

Track a summary of the imputed values — their mean or standard deviation —
across iterations and check that it has plateaued. n_iter_ tells you
whether it stopped on the tolerance or simply hit max_iter; the latter
means it had not converged.
